extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of architectural history; architects, art historians, and travelers interested in Venetian Gothic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and evaluative criteria for identifying, dating, and judging Venetian window types, tracery, ornament, materials, and architectural details (Byzantine → Gothic transitions). Useful for architectural historians, restorers, and comparative analysts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window orders (second, third, fourth, fifth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of window forms into orders (second, third, fourth, fifth) with distinct mouldings and arrangements; the fifth order being a combination of the third and fourth and the nearest approximation to a perfect Gothic form in Venice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the order system to identify chronological and stylistic position: second and third orders contemporaneous; fourth occurs initially in pairs with simple mouldings then enriches; fifth order combines elements of third and fourth and characterizes the early Gothic period. Compare groups in Plates XIV–XVIII for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of specific fourth-order variants (4a–4e)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth order shows several ordinary conditions and arch-line changes: 4a and 4b (early Venetian), 4c (later Venice), 4d (piquant condition with bold projected cusp common to Venice and Verona), 4e (early Veronese).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine provenance and relative dating by matching moulding and cusp projection to these variants; 4d’s projected cusp is diagnostic of a later, more fantastic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusp condition as an age indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The solidity or perforation of the cusp indicates relative age: 'the more solid it is, the more ancient,' while perforated (emaciated) cusps are decorative and appear later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect cusp thickness: solid cusps suggest older/structural use (bearing traceries), perforated/slender cusps suggest later decorative use (upper traceries). Use in conjunction with other points for dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of arches and detachment of shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: The great depth of arches and clear detaching of shafts from the glass behind (shafts set forward from glazing) is a notable characteristic of some Venetian windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining a window, note arch depth and whether shafts are distinct from glazing plane; deep arches with detached shafts imply earlier construction and different glazing attachment (glass set behind shafts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and expressive potential of brick (moulded bricks and terra-cotta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brick is used not merely structurally but expressively: moulded in clay by hand into exquisite mouldings, cast bricks for roll mouldings, bricks wrought into tracery and flower-work as fine as raised patterns on china; terra-cotta as softer material for ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate brickwork quality by checking for hand-moulded uniqueness (no two pieces identical), variety of sizes/strengths, and decorative uses (arch voussoirs, plinths, tracery). The author advocates learning brick usage before marble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trefoiled brick windows and construction method
rubrics_metrics.description: Trefoiled windows made entirely of brick with the trefoils cut out of radiating bricks; central shaft and capital often in Istrian stone; roll moulding formed of cast bricks ground to meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify trefoils cut from radiating bricks and presence of stone central shaft; note simple capitals and lack of bases, plinth projection—these signal early transitional Gothic in humble houses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine insertion and use of inlaid alabaster/marble sheets
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine ornamentation in Venetian palaces appears as inlaid sculptures and variegated alabasters set in the wall; intermediate spaces are covered with sheets of marble bounded by a dentil moulding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for inlaid panels of alabaster or marble between windows and dentil mouldings as signs of Byzantine influence/earlier phases; contrast with later facades where such ornament vanishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition from Byzantine to Gothic ornament (loss of sculpture, move to colour and purity)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the 13th century there is an increase of simplicity: Byzantine rich capitals and wall sculptures give place to a purer, more severe type; colour (alabaster, serpentine, veined marbles) and foliated capitals remain while sculpture largely vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dating or critiquing façades, note the disappearance of sculptural relief and the reliance on coloured marbles and simpler foliate carving as indicative of transitional Gothic tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration of interval between arches (spandrils and tracery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods experimented: spandrils filled by emblems (e.g., the four Evangelists) or by intricate quattrofoil tracery; the Ducal Palace arcade arrangement later became the standard model for important Venetian works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess interval decoration type—figural reliefs vs. quatrefoil tracery—to establish rarity/uniqueness and influence (e.g., Ponte del Forner, Palazzo Cicogna vs. Ducal Palace model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archivolt sculpture program (months and zodiacal signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archivolt sculpture (St. Mark's entrance) personifies the months with representative labours and zodiac signs; sequence and regional variations reflect climate and agricultural systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read archivolt sequences iconographically: identify month labour (e.g., January carrying wood, February warming feet, March as warrior) and zodiac signs; compare with Northern manuscript calendars for regional differences and dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrances: Byzantine gates vs Gothic archivolts and subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine entrances are great semicircular arches with rich sculptured archivolts of grotesques; the Gothic central entrance of St. Mark's exhibits subjects 'altogether Gothic in feeling'—months and life scenes—showing Gothic spirit entering before formal change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate entrance type (grand water-gate vs door), arch shape (semicircular vs pointed/archivolt series), and sculptural program to determine stylistic influence and the moment of Gothic penetration into Byzantine forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and placement of balconies and casements
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller balconies between great shafts are original and characteristic in certain fifth-order windows; lateral balconies may be restorations; casements can be fitted to pointed arches without structural compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish original balconies by material/connection to shafts; beware restored lateral balconies. Note that pointed arches permit varied infill (sashes, casements) once arching is structurally secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural advantage of pointed arch over square lintel
rubrics_metrics.description: The pointed arch (Gothic) is the best and strongest building form compared with the square lintel of the common window; square heads are weakest and prone to failure even when well-constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing building stability, prefer or advocate pointed arches for spanning openings in imperfect materials; watch for fissures and collapses above square lintels as anti-patterns of weak construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat enriched architrave and its Byzantine connection
rubrics_metrics.description: A flat but highly enriched architrave (used in some Venetian windows) connects these Gothic forms with Byzantine work and is a recurring element in early transitional windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify enriched architraves as evidence of Byzantine-Gothic hybridization; consult 'Archivolt' discussion for further connection and examples (Plate XVII figs. 1 and 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization law in palace composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring compositional law: central shaft with pilasters on each side and wall beyond—the system of centralization seen even in humble dwellings mirroring larger palaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence of a central shaft flanked by pilasters and projecting plinths as an indicator of adherence to larger-palace compositional rules, even in lower-order houses; this is an architectural 'law' to note when comparing building scales.
